Budgets are MEASURED, not guessed: arm/measure_range.py sweeps each joint from the resting pose against the MuJoCo checker and reports where it stops being free (joint2 +38 to the clamp zone, joint3 free across its whole range, joint4 +94, joint5 -103/+51, joint6 -131/+108). WHAT EACH GESTURE LOOKS LIKE NOW (hardware, relative offsets, joint1 = 0 throughout):
- wake, 20.0s (startup showpiece): unfolds and rises high (joint3 sweeps 55 deg), reaches out and extends the forearm to -45, then looks around WITH ITS WRIST — joint5/joint6 roll +/-25-30 deg each way, like a head turning, since the base cannot — stretches to full extension, closes and opens the jaws, folds back down. Peak 24 deg/s.
- attention, 12.5s: lifts sharply (joint3 +35), pitches forward, NODS on joint3/joint4, one clamp of the jaws, settles. The nod is what reads as 'I want you' without a base turn. Peak 14 deg/s.
- decline, 13.3s: a slow 'no' done with the WRIST — raises to a speaking pose, then joint5/joint6 counter-rotate +/-28 deg through two cycles so the hand shakes at the end of a still forearm. Peak 25.5 deg/s, fastest in the set.
- point_screen, 9.0s: rears up and reaches toward the screen (joint3 48, forearm -42, wrist rolled 20) and HOLDS 2s. The pointing is the extension, not a yaw. Peak 13.7 deg/s.
- attempt, 14.0s: rises, reaches well out and down (joint4 -44), closes the jaws, LIFTS 8 deg as if testing whether it got the thing, lets go, withdraws. Peak 13.3 deg/s.
- task_demo, 16.0s: rises to 45, extends to -40 with a 20 deg wrist set, lowers onto the spot, closes, lifts clear, releases, folds back. Peak 13.3 deg/s.
All six once = 84.8s. Every one verified live at 25% then 100% amplitude: 1.00x scheduled timing on all six, resyncs<=1, failures=0. The first full-range run printed a stand-clear warning and paused 5 seconds for the human.

SHOW-MUST-GO-ON HARDENING (the CANable dropped off USB twice today, so this is the weak point): ONE automatic in-place bus recovery per H2's triage, then a single well-defined exception. hw_backend._recover_bus_once() rebuilds the bus via arm.reconnect() and probes whether a FRESH handle gets replies — if it does, the host controller had gone bus-off and the arm was fine (this is the macOS failure that masquerades as 'the CANable needs a replug'), so it runs recover_stale_motors() + enable() and carries on; if a fresh handle hears nothing, the arm is genuinely unpowered and it refuses to pretend otherwise. Bounded by RECOVERY_BUDGET_S = 5s, used at most once per session, wired into both connect() and the motion streamer. When it fails, everything raises ONE exception, hw_backend.ArmUnavailable (ArmUnhealthy is kept as an alias), whose message tells the operator to run precheck and tells the demo it can continue without motion. AGENT F: catch hw_backend.ArmUnavailable around arm calls and keep the show running.

RECOVERY VERIFIED BY TEST, not by unplugging anything: monkeypatched can_compat.open_bus to simulate a dead adapter and a silent arm. Four cases pass — adapter gone raises ArmUnavailable in 0.00s with an actionable message; host-side bus-off recovers in place with reconnect/recover_stale_motors/enable each called exactly once; a second attempt is refused (one pass only); a silent bus fails recovery WITHOUT enabling motors.

SELF-COLLISION IS NO LONGER A CAVEAT. R1's official i2rt yam_pro URDF+MJCF plus mujoco 3.12 means yam.environment.ArmSafetyChecker constructs. arm/verify_poses.py checks every waypoint AND every interpolated segment; hw_backend.verify_self_collision_free() now runs automatically inside validate_hardware_motion() on every prepared setpoint stream before a frame is sent, so future gestures are checked without anyone remembering to. Live runs report 'self-collision-free at 92-162 sampled poses (official i2rt model)'. If the model files ever go missing it warns loudly rather than silently downgrading to 'assumed safe'.

HONEST LIMIT ON THE CLAMP CHECK: yam.mapping.base_clamps() describes the two 25mm clamps by hand, but ArmSafetyChecker's environment test uses conservative link-sized spheres (up to 102mm radius) against a 30mm margin, and this arm rests FOLDED with every link between z=0.086 and z=0.266 — inside that margin. Run absolutely it calls the arm's own power-up resting pose a collision, which is false; Boris excludes the base link for exactly this reason. So the clamp check is RELATIVE: a gesture passes only if it never comes closer to the clamps than the arm already is at rest. All five pass at -10mm vs rest -10mm, i.e. no closer. That is a regression test, not proof of clearance, and nothing else on the table is modelled at all — the human watching remains the authority on the rest of the workspace.

LIMITS RAISED, WITH THE AUTHORIZATION CITED IN THE CODE: HW_MAX_EXCURSION_DEG 5 -> 30, with per-joint exceptions HW_PER_JOINT_EXCURSION_DEG = {joint2: 15, joint3: 25} — joint2 stays tight against its documented ~105 deg base-collision trap, joint3 gets the largest budget because yam.arm records it as self-collision-free across its whole range from home, and it does the visible lifting. Added HW_SLOW_SPEED_DEG_S = 15.0, a hard slow-motion ceiling enforced on the prepared stream and well under the 34.4 deg/s velocity cap, so 'do it slow' is checked rather than trusted. The sim pick-and-place is still refused on hardware (negative control in smoke).

RAMPED TESTING IS A REAL FEATURE, NOT A ONE-OFF: motion.scale_amplitude() shrinks a relative gesture's offsets without touching its timing, so a 25% pass is also slower in deg/s and strictly safer than the full one. Exposed as arm_io.gesture(name, amplitude=0.25) and replay(..., amplitude=). Relative frames only — it refuses on absolute trajectories, where scaling would mean moving toward the origin.

BUG FIXED THIS ROUND: interpolating a joint back to its starting value lands at -0.050000000000000710 rather than -0.05, which read as a soft-limit violation against the rest-pose tolerance and refused every gesture. Added model.LIMIT_EPSILON_DEG = 1e-6.

Boris's RRT planner + GuardedExecutor were considered and NOT adopted: these are short authored gestures in free space near a known resting pose, already verified pose-by-pose against the same collision model the planner would use, so planning adds a dependency and a failure mode without changing what the arm does. GuardedExecutor's torque-residual contact detection is the piece worth revisiting if gestures ever move near objects.

EARLIER HISTORY BELOW.

READ THE HARDWARE STATUS FIELD FIRST. The arm was brought up, moved, and smoke-tested green on real hardware. Afterwards the CANable2 vanished from USB: pyusb finds 0 devices matching 0x1D50:0x606F, GsUsb.scan() returns 0, and `ioreg -p IOUSB -w0 -l | grep -i canable` is empty, so macOS does not see the adapter at all. hwsupport/triage.py rates this 'stop_the_demo — USB enumeration failure, upstream of anything CAN-protocol related; check the USB cable to the CANable', and says the agent must not replug it. USER ACTION REQUIRED: reseat the CANable's USB cable (and its CAN cable at the arm), then re-run `.venv/bin/python arm/hw_bringup.py --read-only`, which now reports 'No adapter' and stops cleanly instead of crashing. Nothing else is needed — no code change is pending on this.

Possible self-inflicted trigger, disclosed: my shutdown() briefly called usb.util.dispose_resources() on the scanned adapter to release the interface. The disappearance happened later in that same session. I cannot prove causation, but the call was never necessary (open_bus()'s single-bus-per-process rule already fixes the double-claim, and yam/can_compat.py patches out the macOS usb.reset() problem), so it has been REMOVED. Boris independently documents the CANable vanishing and re-enumerating under load, so it may equally be that.

WHAT RAN ON THE REAL ARM (all of it, twice: once at 50%/25% and once at 100%): enable + keep-alive, home(), gesture attention, decline, point_screen, replay(task_demo). Zero CAN failures across both runs (failures=0, resyncs=0 then 2). Motor temperatures 27-32C throughout. Measured: keep-alive streams at 82-83 Hz (a 7-joint tick costs ~12ms; the latch threshold in yam.arm is 20 Hz with 0.3-0.4s gaps, so there is wide margin), and every motion ran at 1.00x its scheduled duration.

TIMING BUG FOUND AND FIXED ON HARDWARE: the first run took 86s for an 18s gesture (4.8x). Cause was one lock covering both the ~8ms CAN exchange and the target update, so each of 1801 setpoint sends queued behind a bus transaction. Split into _bus_lock and _target_lock; every motion now measures 1.00x. This is why the motion streamer still exists alongside H1's Keepalive.

BRING-UP FINDINGS: (1) verify_against_yam() FIRED on the first hardware run and blocked bring-up before any bus traffic — Boris's sync replaced SafetyLimits.max_step_per_tick (0.02 rad/tick) with max_joint_speed (2.0 rad/s), and arm/model.py still mirrored the old constant. The numeric cap is unchanged (0.02 x 100 Hz = 2.0 rad/s) but it is now anchored to the constant that actually governs. The mirror check paid for itself. (2) All six arm joints were carrying the benign 0xD comms-lost latch at first contact; the gripper read 'disabled'. connect()'s single recover_stale_motors()/clear_errors() pass cleared it every time. (3) Boris's documented rest-position epsilon is real: joint2/joint3 rest at -0.01 deg, just below their 0.0 bound, and my limit check refused the arm's own resting pose until check_limits() grew a REST_LIMIT_TOLERANCE_DEG plus a no-worsening rule against the base pose. (4) The gripper's resting opening MOVES between sessions (99.1% then 78.6% then 76%) because its open stop is compliant — which is exactly why the hardware gestures are authored as relative offsets. (5) libusb allows one interface claim per process: a read-only probe that closed its own bus made connect() fail with 'Access denied'. The backend now owns one bus for the process and probe_passive() shares it.

HARDWARE GESTURE TABLE (operator's rule: arm essentially still, motion is the jaws): arm/gestures/hardware/*.json, selected automatically by the same FACTS flag that picks the backend — callers still just say gesture('decline'). They are RELATIVE offsets from whatever pose the arm is resting in, and they CLOSE the jaws (this arm rests nearly open). attention = one clamp + 3 deg of joint6, 5.8s. decline = three clamp pulses + 2 deg joint6 shake, 9.0s. point_screen = holds pose, clamps once and holds while the screen is read, 9.5s — it does NOT turn toward the screen, that would be a joint1 sweep. task_demo = a slow close-hold-open gripper cycle at the current pose, 7.0s, NOT a pick-and-place. Enforced in code, not just in the JSON: hw_backend.validate_hardware_motion() checks the whole prepared setpoint stream before the first frame and refuses anything moving an arm joint more than 5.0 deg from the start pose or the gripper faster than 12 %/s. Negative control in the smoke test: the sim's pick-and-place task_demo IS refused on hardware ('joint1 moves 27.9 deg...'). Gripper commands go through Boris's calibrated stops (GRIPPER_CLOSED/OPEN_POSITION) at gain_scale 0.5 and his 0.6 Nm (~41 N) torque ceiling.

home() ON HARDWARE DOES NOT SWEEP. It settles and holds the pose the arm is already in, and says so. model.HOME_POSE_DEG was measured on another day in another spot; driving to it from an unknown pose is exactly the large unattended motion the rules forbid. recover_home() likewise resumes the hold rather than travelling. run_demo.py calls home() at setup and is unaffected.

H1 KEEPALIVE INTEGRATED (their finding was correct and would have ended the demo): hwsupport.keepalive.Keepalive now holds the pose between motions with its single-pass 0xD recovery; the backend's own streamer drives setpoints during a motion. They alternate and are NEVER on the bus together — begin_motion() calls keepalive.pause() (a real barrier) before starting the motion streamer, end_motion() and hold() stop it and call resume(). Freeze-on-interrupt now hands the frozen pose to the keepalive, so a frozen arm keeps its recovery policy. The motion streamer got the same one-pass policy, importing H1's COMMS_LOST_TEXT rather than restating the error text so it cannot drift from yam.dm_motor. Not adopted: driving motion through Keepalive itself, because it holds a re-read pose rather than accepting setpoints, and commanding from the motion thread reintroduces the 4.8x stretch.

ARM_FORCE_SIM ADDED for F: set it and arm_io runs the simulator even with an arm attached (`ARM_FORCE_SIM=1 ... --rehearse`). It only ever moves in the safe direction — there is deliberately no variable that forces hardware ON, since a stale shell variable must never outrank FACTS.md.

EDIT TO F's FILE (demo/run_demo.py, one function): gate() no longer blocks for a dedicated keypress when is_motion=True — it prints the [ARM] line and returns 'go', so motions run when their beat reaches them, per the operator's override. Beat pacing on SPACE is untouched, every non-motion step still waits, 'h' still recovers, and Ctrl-C is still the e-stop. F should re-read this before rehearsal. F should also know the hardware beat timings differ from the sim ones its banners quote: task_demo is 7.0s on hardware (banner says ~19.4s), attention 5.8s (3.4s), decline 9.0s (7.4s), point_screen 9.5s (7.4s).

STILL NOT VERIFIABLE: self-collision. yam.environment.ArmSafetyChecker needs mujoco and the i2rt URDF; neither is on this machine (../i2rt does not exist). The mitigation is structural rather than a check — every hardware pose is within 5 deg of a pose the arm is already resting in, so it cannot reach a collision it is not already in, and joint2 (the documented base-collision trap at ~105 deg) moves at most 3 deg. Stated plainly for the build card.
